title: Research
text:
My current book project, Affective Drift and Englishness from Woolf to Brexit: Literature, Film, and Media, examines how Englishness has been shaped through emotional practices of restraint, endurance, and belonging. The project traces changing forms of English identity from modernist literature to contemporary heritage media and post-Brexit culture.
My broader research explores diaspora narratives, postcolonial experiences of feeling, heritage genres, and streaming media. I study how cultural forms organize experiences of memory, belonging, and social difference.

title: Teaching
text: I view literature, media, and writing as opportunities for students to examine how narratives shape ideas of identity, history, and social experience. In my classroom, students learn to navigate texts critically across diverse media and develop the ability to connect formal structures to broader cultural dynamics. My pedagogy emphasizes close reading, process-oriented drafting, and scaffolded assignment sequences that guide students from initial inquiry to rigorous, research-integrated arguments. I have gained extensive experience as an Instructor of Record at Binghamton University, and I am now expanding this pedagogy into an international setting in Seoul, teaching a diverse student body.

title: Teaching
text:
Courses Taught

Literature and Culture


British Fiction and Film


This course examines how British literary classics of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries have been adapted since WWII, in dialogue with Thatcherism, the heritage industry, colonialism, and the question of Englishness and Britishness. Students ask what a heritage adaptation keeps of its source and what it must discard to survive the crossing from page to screen, treating adaptation as a lens for understanding how originals persist within a changing cultural environment. The course pairs close reading with attention to the industries and politics that decide which pasts get restaged.




Korean Modern Literature and Film


This course introduces modern Korean history through Korean fiction and film, tracing how war and division, industrialization, democratization, and diaspora have taken different aesthetic form across decades. Five thematic units pair an original Korean literary text with a related film or television adaptation, from Lee Beomseon’s postwar fiction to globally circulated titles such as Parasite, Squid Game, and Minari, asking what changes when a national trauma travels from the page to a global screen. Students develop skills in comparative literary and cinematic analysis.




Contesting America: Culture, Media, and Society


This course asks how American exceptionalism survives its own contradictions, tracing how a founding narrative of free and equal nationhood persists in public culture even as race, class, gender, and political polarization visibly strain it. Students read literature, speeches, essays, journalism, and social media material through a light grounding in postcolonial and affect theory, examining the cultural work the myth performs regardless of its factual truth. Four issue-based units, race and citizenship, class and mobility, gender and generation, and populism and gun culture, converge in a closing unit on multiculturalism.





Film and Media


Best Picture: Oscar Winners


This course examines how the Academy Awards function simultaneously as an aesthetic judgment and a political instrument, tracing how recent Best Picture and Best Adapted Screenplay winners have negotiated race, gender, ethnicity, and disability under sustained public pressure, including the #OscarSoWhite reckoning. Students ask whether recognition redistributes power or absorbs critique into the same structures it appears to challenge. The course pairs close textual analysis with attention to the institutional and promotional apparatus that shapes who wins.




Hip-Hop: Culture of Voice


This course explores hip-hop’s relationship to gender, sexuality, race, and social issues across music, film, lyrics, and new media, tracing its evolution from a musical genre into a broader cultural movement. Students ask what hip-hop’s spirit consists of, how identity is contested and negotiated within it, and how commercialization has changed who gets to speak and who is spoken for. The course pays close attention to the visual, examining what role image and performance play alongside sound.





Academic Writing


Inquiry and Academic Writing


This inquiry-driven course helps first-year students become rigorous researchers, effective writers, and confident speakers. Through a sequence of connected assignments, students learn to navigate diverse rhetorical contexts, avoid confirmation bias through robust research, and build original arguments for academic and civic audiences. The curriculum centers on process-oriented drafting, peer collaboration, and critical source integration, preparing students for the intellectual demands of college and beyond.




Bridging Academic Writing


This writing-intensive course engages students in the full cycle of composition, moving from initial invention to global and local revision. Students learn to critique their own and others’ writing while analyzing cultural myths that inform identity and society. By employing scaffolded writing assignments and direct source integration, the course bridges close reading with rigorous, research-backed cultural analysis, fostering both critical thinkers and effective communicators.

title: Bora Kang
text:
I am a scholar of Anglophone literature specializing in modern and contemporary British fiction, film, and media culture. I received my Ph.D. in English from Binghamton University. My research investigates the intersection of literary form and felt experience, asking how narrative structures and public institutions organize emotion, belonging, and national identity, within Britain and in the overseas markets where Englishness now sells.
I gather this work under one phrase: Surplus Englishness. The British empire contracted, while the structure of feeling that sustained it had been built at imperial scale; the remainder is a surplus that the post-imperial nation cannot absorb on its own. My first book studies this surplus on the island itself. Its central concept, affective drift, names the persistence of national feeling through rhythm, repetition, and literary form when narrative closure fails to arrive. The monograph, Affective Drift and Englishness from Woolf to Brexit: Literature, Film, and Media, follows the process across a century of crises: it moves through Woolf, Lawrence, and Ishiguro, takes up heritage screen media, and arrives at Ali Smith’s Brexit novels.
My second project follows this question outward: how does the rest of the world learn to feel England? The unabsorbed surplus flows outward, and Englishness takes on new cultural lives beyond the reach of the former empire, in places that owe it nothing. One question thus divides along two axes: the first book measures how long the feeling lasts, and this project measures how far it can travel. I call the condition affective extraterritoriality: national feeling operating outside the territory, and outside the jurisdiction, of the state that produced it. I trace its residue through the screens, marketplaces, and classrooms where England continues to acquire meaning as an object of desire. I work from a double position: near enough to read these worlds from inside their own idiom, and far enough outside to see the system that connects them.
